6.question: Did quantum mechanics end science's claim to describe reality itself — or just expose the wrong picture of it?
6.why: A century after Copenhagen, the foundations argument is livelier than it has been since Bohr and Einstein: hidden-variable, many-worlds and informational readings all claim the same experiments. What is at stake is whether physics describes a world or only our knowledge of one.

sides.label: Accept the Copenhagen settlement: physics predicts measurements, not a picture of reality
points: The formalism is confirmed to extraordinary precision; the demand for an underlying picture adds nothing testable.
Bell's theorem and its experiments rule out the most natural 'realist' escape routes (local hidden variables).
Insisting on a God's-eye view smuggles in a classical prejudice the theory itself undermined.
objections: 'Shut up and calculate' is not an interpretation; it leaves the measurement problem — when and why collapse happens — unanswered.
Every experiment presupposes a real apparatus, real records and real outcomes; instrumentalism helps itself to that reality.
Predictive success has never before been treated as a reason to stop asking what a theory is about.

sides.label: Keep realism: there is a definite world, and the theory is incomplete (Einstein's line)
points: Pilot-wave (de Broglie–Bohm) theory reproduces all quantum predictions with particles that always have positions — so realism is not refuted, only unfashionable.
Bell excludes local hidden variables; non-local ones, or theories that give up 'statistical independence' (superdeterminism), remain open and possibly testable.
A theory of the world should say what exists between measurements; otherwise 'measurement' is an undefined primitive.
objections: Non-locality sits awkwardly with relativity, and hidden-variable theories have so far made no distinctive confirmed prediction.
Superdeterminism is accused of undermining the very idea of free experimental choice — and with it, of experiment.
Adding unobservable structure to save a picture is exactly what critics call emotional attachment to classical reality.

sides.label: Take the theory literally: the wavefunction never collapses (many worlds)
points: No collapse postulate, no special role for observers, no non-locality — the equations alone.
Decoherence explains why we see one outcome without adding anything to the theory.
objections: It struggles to say what probability means when every outcome happens.
An uncountable infinity of worlds is a heavy price; critics call it the most reckless idea in physics.

speakers.name: Philip Ball
speakers.stance: In Beyond Weird he argues quantum mechanics is best read as a theory about information and what can be known; he has been sharply critical of many-worlds. Expect him to resist both naive realism and the claim that the theory is 'just weird'.

speakers.name: Antony Valentini
speakers.stance: A leading developer of de Broglie–Bohm pilot-wave theory; has argued the universe may carry traces of 'quantum non-equilibrium' that would make hidden variables detectable, for instance in the cosmic microwave background. Expect the case that realism was never refuted.

speakers.name: Sabine Hossenfelder
speakers.stance: Author of Lost in Math and Existential Physics; has argued quantum mechanics is incomplete, defended superdeterminism as a live option, and dismissed many-worlds as untestable. Expect scepticism towards interpretations that make no new predictions.

speakers.name: Bjorn Ekeberg
speakers.stance: Hosts. Philosopher of science whose Metaphysical Experiments questions the metaphysical assumptions behind physical cosmology.

questions: What experiment, even in principle, would distinguish your interpretation from the others?
If physics only predicts measurements, what is a measurement — and who or what performs one?
Is 'the universe is real and describable' a scientific hypothesis or a precondition for doing science at all?

reading.title: Beyond Weird
reading.note: Ball's own account of what the theory does and doesn't say.

reading.title: Existential Physics
reading.note: Chapter on whether the universe is deterministic sets up her position.

reading.title: Quantum Mechanics: Myths and Facts
reading.note: A short, sober list of what is and isn't settled — good armour against slogans.

terms.def: Bohr and Heisenberg's view: the theory gives probabilities for measurement outcomes; asking what happens in between is meaningless.
Extra quantities, not in the standard theory, that would fix outcomes in advance — Einstein's hope, Bohm's construction.
No theory that is both local and realist can reproduce quantum correlations; experiments since 1982 confirm the quantum side.
Escapes Bell by denying that measurement settings are independent of the system measured.

7.question: Is free trade the engine of the greatest rise in living standards in history — or a doctrine that only the already-dominant can afford?
7.why: Tariffs are back at the centre of American policy, the EU and China are openly industrial-strategists, and the post-1945 trade order is being renegotiated in real time. The argument is no longer academic: it decides where factories, jobs and alliances go.

sides.label: Free trade works: comparative advantage, cheaper goods, faster growth for everyone who opens up
points: The 70 years of falling tariffs coincided with the fastest fall in global poverty ever recorded; East Asia's growth ran on exporting into open markets.
Tariffs are a tax on your own consumers and on the firms that import components; retaliation makes everyone poorer.
Protection breeds complacent industries and lobbying; the losers from trade are better helped with transfers and retraining than with walls.
objections: The textbook case assumes full employment and immobile capital; when capital moves, comparative advantage stops guaranteeing shared gains.
The 'China shock' concentrated losses in particular towns for decades, and the promised compensation rarely arrived.
Historically, nearly every industrial economy — Britain, the US, Germany, Korea — protected its infant industries first and preached free trade afterwards.

sides.label: Trade is a tool, not a creed: strategic protection and industrial policy built the winners
points: Hamilton's America, Bismarck's Germany, MITI's Japan and Korea's chaebol all grew behind tariffs and state-picked champions.
Security, resilience and technological sovereignty (semiconductors, energy, pharmaceuticals) are legitimate goals that pure efficiency ignores.
Free-trade orthodoxy served the hegemon of the day; the rules were written by whoever was already ahead.
objections: For every Korea there is an Argentina or an India before 1991: protection more often produced stagnation and rent-seeking.
Governments are poor at picking winners; the successes are remembered, the expensive failures forgotten.
Protectionism invites retaliation and blocs; the 1930s show where a tariff war ends.

speakers.name: Steve Keen
speakers.stance: Heterodox economist (Debunking Economics) who has argued that the Ricardian case for free trade collapses once capital is mobile and that mainstream trade theory ignores real-world assumptions. Expect the sharpest attack on the orthodoxy.

speakers.name: Jeremy Hunt
speakers.stance: Former Chancellor; as a Conservative minister championed post-Brexit trade agreements. Likely to defend open trade in principle while conceding security and China-related exceptions.

speakers.name: Gillian Tett
speakers.stance: FT columnist and anthropologist who has written on the shift from the 'Washington consensus' to geoeconomics. Likely to argue the assumptions behind free trade have changed rather than to take a purist side.

speakers.name: Martin Wolf
speakers.stance: FT chief economics commentator and one of globalisation's most prominent defenders (Why Globalization Works; The Crisis of Democratic Capitalism), strongly critical of Trump-era tariffs. Expect the fullest case for openness, with acknowledgement of the China shock.

speakers.name: Hilary Lawson
speakers.stance: Hosts. Founder of the festival and the Institute of Art and Ideas.

questions: Which country's growth story is the exception to your rule — and why doesn't it count?
If the losers from trade could have been compensated but weren't, is that a failure of trade or of politics?
Is a tariff for national security different in kind from a tariff to protect jobs, or just better branded?

reading.title: Why Globalization Works
reading.note: The classic statement of the case he'll be defending.

reading.title: Kicking Away the Ladder
reading.note: The historical case that rich countries protected first and preached later — the backbone of Keen's side.

reading.title: 'The China Shock'
reading.note: The study everyone cites on concentrated losses from import competition.

terms.def: Ricardo's argument that countries gain by specialising in what they do relatively best, even if another country does everything better.
Temporary protection lets a new industry reach scale before facing established foreign rivals.
Government steering of particular sectors through subsidies, procurement, protection or state ownership.

12.question: Have we all been recruited into a cult of the online — and can the tools that get people out of cults get us out?
12.why: This is a conversation rather than a formal debate: Louis Theroux has spent thirty years inside Scientology, Westboro Baptist and the far right. The proposal is to turn that lens on ordinary scrolling, arguing and belonging.

sides.label: The internet really does work like a cult
points: The classic markers — us-versus-them, love-bombing on arrival, thought-terminating clichés, escalating commitment, punishment for leaving — map neatly onto online communities and fandoms.
Attention-farming platforms are designed to be hard to leave; certainty and outrage are rewarded, doubt is not.
Productivity culture is the same mechanism pointed at the self: optimise everything, never simply not know.
objections: Cults have leaders, walls and total control; the internet has an exit button and a billion competing groups.
The analogy flatters us: 'we were groomed' removes responsibility for what we chose to read and join.
Most people use the internet for train times and recipes; the pathological cases make the story, not the norm.

sides.label: The cult frame misleads — this is ordinary human tribalism with a new medium
points: Every mass medium was accused of manufacturing madness: novels, radio, television, video games.
Belonging, status and outrage predate platforms; the medium amplifies but does not create them.
The remedy is boring: media literacy, friction, and better institutions — not deprogramming.
objections: Scale and personalisation are new: no previous medium tailored a private feed of certainty to each person.
Radicalisation pipelines are documented; 'it was always thus' is not an answer to a measured change.

speakers.name: Louis Theroux
speakers.stance: Documentary-maker known for immersive, non-judgemental portraits of extreme groups (Scientology, the Westboro Baptist Church, US far right). Expect anecdotes on how people get pulled in and out, and reluctance to condemn from a distance.

speakers.name: Robin Clyfan
speakers.stance: Hosts, for Sage & Jester, the organisation behind the event.

questions: What is the single feature of a cult that the internet lacks — and does that make the analogy break or just wobble?
In your films, what actually got people out? Was it argument, or something else?
What would a healthy version of online belonging look like — not just less of the bad kind?

reading.title: Thought Reform and the Psychology of Totalism
reading.note: The eight criteria of thought reform that every 'is it a cult?' checklist descends from.

reading.title: Cultish: The Language of Fanaticism
reading.note: Argues cult language runs from SoulCycle to Silicon Valley.

reading.title: Louis Theroux: My Scientology Movie
reading.note: His method in action.

terms.def: A stock phrase that ends inquiry rather than answering it — Lifton's term, now applied to online slogans.
Business models where the product is your attention, sold to advertisers, so engagement is optimised over wellbeing.

13.question: Is there a correct way to tell good from evil — or only competing codes that history keeps overturning?
13.why: Moral confidence is everywhere in politics while moral agreement is nowhere. If yesterday's certainties (slavery, eugenics) were monstrous, what licenses today's? The debate pits universal principles against the record of how they've been used.

sides.label: Morality is discovered, not invented: some things are simply wrong, everywhere and always
points: We do not say slavery became wrong; we say it always was and people failed to see it — that only makes sense if there is something to see.
Human rights, international law and the prohibition of genocide rest on the claim of universal wrongs; relativism disarms exactly the people who most need protection.
Disagreement about hard cases no more shows there is no moral truth than disagreement in science shows there are no facts.
objections: Every era's confident universalism turned out to be its own prejudices in Sunday clothes — including, critics say, today's.
Which universal principle? Kant, Mill and the Torah give different answers, and each generates monstrous verdicts in some scenario.
'Discovered' by whom, with what faculty? Moral perception has no instrument to correct it the way telescopes correct sight.

sides.label: Moral codes are human, historical and tied to power — there is no view from nowhere
points: Codes have always served someone: the Greeks' natural slavery, Manifest Destiny, the Supreme Court's eugenics — each was 'reason' at the time.
Rigid principles produce perverse outcomes in edge cases; ethics is better understood as judgement within a tradition than as calculation from an axiom.
Giving up the single correct code doesn't mean anything goes; it means arguing, revising, and owning our choices.
objections: If it's all codes and power, the critic has no standing to call the eugenics ruling wrong rather than merely different.
Relativism is self-refuting when it condemns colonialism or oppression — it needs the universal standard it denies.
Traditions of judgement still smuggle in principles; they just refuse to state them.

speakers.name: Tommy Curry
speakers.stance: Critical race theorist (The Man-Not) who has argued that Western moral and political theory was built around racial hierarchy. Expect the case that codes have served power and that universalism has a history worth suspecting.

speakers.name: Norman Finkelstein
speakers.stance: Political scientist known for uncompromising arguments about international law and human rights, most recently on Gaza. Despite the 'controversial' billing, his method is morally absolutist: expect him to insist that some acts are wrong on any code.

speakers.name: Thangam Debbonaire
speakers.stance: Labour peer and former shadow culture secretary. Likely to defend workable rules — rights frameworks, institutions — as the practical form moral principle takes, while accepting that they evolve.

speakers.name: Jay Shapiro
speakers.stance: Hosts. Philosopher and podcaster (Dilemma).

questions: Name one thing you think is wrong in every possible society. What makes it different from the things past societies were sure about?
If moral codes serve power, what serves the powerless — and isn't that a moral claim?
When a principle gives a monstrous verdict in a thought experiment, is that a problem with the principle or with the experiment?

reading.title: After Virtue
reading.note: The influential argument that modern moral debate is interminable because we inherited fragments of incompatible traditions.

reading.title: The Man-Not
reading.note: Curry's position on race, theory and who counts.

reading.title: Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong
reading.note: The classic case that moral values are made, not found — and why that needn't be nihilism.

terms.def: The view that there are moral facts independent of anyone's beliefs or cultures.
Right and wrong are relative to a culture or framework; there is no standpoint outside all of them.
Nietzsche's and Foucault's method: explaining a moral idea by the history and interests that produced it.

21.question: Is the United States still winning — and is 'winning' even the right way to think about power between nations?
21.why: China builds warships five times faster; the dollar still settles half of world trade; American alliances look shakier than at any point since 1945. The question shapes everything from Ukraine to Taiwan to European defence budgets.

sides.label: America still leads and can keep leading — if it chooses to
points: Military technology, the dollar, universities, energy independence and demographics all favour the US; China's growth is slowing into an ageing population.
Decline is a choice: retreat from alliances and commitments is what turns relative slippage into absolute loss.
Rivals' strengths are often exaggerated — the Soviet Union also 'overtook' the US in the 1970s, on paper.
objections: Manufacturing capacity, shipbuilding and supply chains now sit in China; wars are won by production, not by the best prototype.
The alliance system depends on trust that recent policy swings have spent.
Primacy has been expensive and often self-defeating (Iraq, Afghanistan); 'lead more' is not a strategy.

sides.label: The unipolar moment is over; the question is how the US adjusts to being one power among several
points: By purchasing-power measures China's economy is already larger; India, Indonesia, Nigeria and Brazil will follow.
The rest of the world is hedging: half of global trade already happens outside the big blocs.
A transactional America accelerates its own decline by treating allies as customers.
objections: Multipolarity in theory has often meant great-power war in practice (1914).
GDP tables are not power: the US still dominates finance, technology standards and the seas.
Prophecies of American decline have a 60-year record of being wrong.

sides.label: 'Winners and losers' is the mistake: security is not a league table
points: Framing relations as a contest makes conflict more likely — the Thucydides trap is a story that can write itself.
Small and middle powers have shown the limits of great-power dominance: Ukraine, Iran, Taiwan's chip leverage.
The problems that matter — climate, pandemics, AI — are not won by any single nation.
objections: Whether or not you think in contests, Beijing and Moscow do; unilateral disarmament of the frame is naive.
Cooperation still requires someone able to enforce rules — which is what hegemony provided.

speakers.name: John Bolton
speakers.stance: Former US National Security Advisor and long-time hawk; has argued for maintaining American primacy through strength and has been openly critical of Trump's deal-making and retreat from allies. Expect no concession that decline is inevitable.

speakers.name: Malcolm Rifkind
speakers.stance: Former UK Foreign Secretary and Defence Secretary, an Atlanticist. Likely to argue that the US remains the indispensable power but only through alliances, and that Europe must do more.

speakers.name: Nicola Sturgeon
speakers.stance: Former First Minister of Scotland. Likely to challenge the winners-and-losers framing itself, speak for smaller nations and multilateralism, and question American reliability.

speakers.name: John Prideaux
speakers.stance: Hosts. The Economist's US editor and host of its Checks and Balance podcast.

questions: What would count as evidence that the US has lost — and has any of it happened yet?
If alliances are America's key strength, what is the plan when allies stop trusting the next election?
Is China's shipbuilding lead a war-fighting advantage or a peacetime statistic?

reading.title: Destined for War
reading.note: The 'Thucydides trap' argument that everyone in this debate will either lean on or attack.

reading.title: The Room Where It Happened
reading.note: Bolton's own account of policy inside the first Trump administration.

reading.title: Has China Won?
reading.note: The strongest recent case for the 'America must adjust' view — Mahbubani speaks in the 17:30 Superpowers debate.

terms.def: Charles Krauthammer's 1990 phrase for post-Cold War American dominance.
A world with several centres of power rather than one or two.
The claim that a rising power and a ruling power tend towards war.

22.question: Will scaling language models ever produce real intelligence — or has the hype outrun what pattern-matching on text can do?
22.why: Trillions of dollars are riding on the assumption that more data and compute keep delivering. If the critics are right that models need a body and a world, the current paradigm peaks soon and a lot of capital is misallocated; if they're wrong, almost every cognitive job changes.

sides.label: Scaling works: the models keep getting more capable and there's no wall in sight
points: Every predicted ceiling so far has been passed; capabilities that were 'impossible for a word predictor' arrived on schedule.
Reasoning, tool use and multimodal input are already being added on top of language; the transformer is a platform, not a dead end.
Intelligence is as intelligence does: if a system solves the problems, arguing it 'doesn't really understand' is a definition, not a discovery.
objections: Human text is finite and largely consumed; synthetic data may not substitute for contact with the world.
Models still fail at simple novel tasks, confabulate, and don't know what they don't know — signs of pattern-matching rather than understanding.
Benchmark gains partly measure contamination and optimisation for the benchmark.

sides.label: Language models are sophisticated word calculators; intelligence needs a world, a body, and goals
points: Meaning is grounded in action and perception; a system that only sees text has no access to what words are about.
Children learn from tiny data with bodies and stakes; the data-hungry approach is evidence of a missing ingredient, not a route to it.
The economics point the same way: when returns diminish, the investment cycle turns into a bubble.
objections: 'Grounding' is asserted more than demonstrated; blind people acquire colour concepts from language alone.
Embodiment can be added — robots run on the same models — so the criticism is about today's products, not the approach.
Every critic's list of what AI can't do has been shrinking for seventy years.

speakers.name: Michael Wooldridge
speakers.stance: Oxford professor of AI and author of The Road to Conscious Machines; has argued that LLMs are remarkable but not on a path to general intelligence, and has been sceptical of existential-risk framing. Expect measured deflation of both hype and doom.

speakers.name: Sabrina Pasterski
speakers.stance: Theoretical physicist (celestial holography). Her published work isn't on AI, so expect a first-principles view on what scaling laws can and cannot promise rather than a fixed position.

speakers.name: Hilary Lawson
speakers.stance: His theory of 'closure' holds that language doesn't mirror the world but is a way of holding it. Expect the argument that models manipulate closures without ever engaging the world they close.

speakers.name: Audrey Borowski
speakers.stance: Cambridge philosopher and historian of Leibniz and the origins of calculating machines. Likely to place today's claims in a 350-year history of promises that reasoning could be mechanised.

speakers.name: Güneş Taylor
speakers.stance: Hosts. Geneticist and science communicator.

questions: What is one task a model would have to do for you to concede it understands — and would you accept it if it did?
If the missing ingredient is a body, why do robotics labs run on the same language models?
Who bears the loss if scaling stalls: investors, or the public services now being built on it?

reading.title: The Road to Conscious Machines
reading.note: His history of AI's cycles of hype and winter.

reading.title: 'On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots'
reading.note: The paper that gave the sceptical side its slogan.

reading.title: 'Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models'
reading.note: Where the belief that bigger keeps getting better came from.

terms.def: The 2017 architecture behind current models: each word is processed in the light of every other, in parallel.
Empirical regularities showing predictable improvement as data, parameters and compute grow.
How symbols in a system come to be about things in the world rather than just other symbols.

24.question: Can you keep Christianity's culture and ethics while dropping its God — or is 'cultural Christianity' an incoherent halfway house?
24.why: Churchgoing keeps falling while Dawkins, Murray and Peterson call themselves cultural Christians and the political right rediscovers religion. Whether the ethics survive the metaphysics is a question about the foundations of Western liberal values themselves.

sides.label: Keep the values, drop the metaphysics: the settlement Tolstoy proposed is workable and honest
points: Equality, human dignity and care for the weak are historically Christian ideas; you can inherit them without believing a man rose from the dead.
Much of Europe already lives this way — cathedrals, carols, Christian festivals and secular law — without visible collapse.
Demanding all-or-nothing hands the tradition to fundamentalists and nationalists.
objections: Values cut from their roots wither within a generation or two: the argument that liberalism is living off inherited capital it cannot replenish.
Without the transcendent claim, 'love thy neighbour' is one preference among others, with no answer to the strong who decline it.
It is parasitic: the cultural Christian enjoys the cathedral while relying on believers to keep it open.

sides.label: Christianity without God is incoherent — either take the claims seriously or let it go
points: Christian ethics is not a list of nice values but a response to a claim about the world; remove the claim and the response has no content.
Treating religion as heritage is condescending to believers and dishonest about what you actually think is true.
The New Right's use of Christian symbols without belief shows exactly where cultural Christianity leads: identity politics in vestments.
objections: Plenty of coherent ethical systems have no god; the incoherence charge proves too much.
Believers have always disagreed about the metaphysics while sharing the practice; the 'real' Christianity is itself contested.
Cultures inherit rituals from beliefs no one holds — nobody thinks December feasts require believing in the sun's rebirth.

speakers.name: David Aaronovitch
speakers.stance: Atheist journalist whose Saturday breakfast talk is on how Christian nationalism is being weaponised on the right. Expect him to reject the supernatural claims and to argue that cultural Christianity is being used as a political identity.

speakers.name: Laila Cunningham
speakers.stance: Reform UK councillor in Westminster and former Conservative, billed as the party's London figurehead. Likely to defend Christianity's cultural and heritage role as part of national identity.

speakers.name: Alister McGrath
speakers.stance: Oxford theologian and Dawkins critic (The Dawkins Delusion). Expect the argument that Christian ethics depends on Christian belief and that cultural Christianity is unstable — a case that oddly agrees with atheists on the incoherence.

speakers.name: Jack Symes
speakers.stance: Hosts. Philosopher and presenter of The Panpsycast.

questions: Name a specifically Christian value that survives if there is no God. What makes it Christian rather than just human?
Is a 'cultural Christian' politician defending a faith or a flag?
If the ethics can't survive the loss of belief, what explains secular Scandinavia?

reading.title: Dominion
reading.note: The case that Western values are Christian to the core, including the values used against Christianity.

reading.title: 'A Confession' and 'What I Believe'
reading.note: The original proposal: keep the Sermon on the Mount, drop the supernatural.

reading.title: The Dawkins Delusion?
reading.note: McGrath's short reply to the New Atheists.

terms.def: Identifying with Christian traditions, art and ethics without believing its doctrines.
Politics that treats a nation's identity as Christian and seeks to entrench that in law and public life.
The claim that modernisation inevitably erodes religion — challenged by the US and much of the global South.

29.question: Is literature's turn to the self — memoir, autofiction, 'my story' — a truer mirror on life, or a narcissism that dissolves the shared stories that held us together?
29.why: Publishers and prizes reward the first person; the epic, the social novel and the invented world look old-fashioned. The argument is about whether 'my truth' can still carry the universal, and whether a culture with only private stories has a common one at all.

sides.label: The personal is the route to the universal: honest particulars reach further than invented generalities
points: Montaigne, Augustine and Wordsworth wrote themselves and are read for what they say about everyone; the self was never a new subject.
Autofiction is a form, not a confession — it uses the self as material exactly as Shakespeare used kings.
The 'universal' stories of the past were often one group's story presented as everyone's; the first person let the excluded speak.
objections: When every story is 'my story', criticism becomes impossible — to doubt the work is to doubt the person.
A literature of experience narrows to what the writer has lived; imagination and research atrophy.
The market rewards the personal because it is cheap to brand; that is an economic fact, not an aesthetic one.

sides.label: The self is a small subject: epic, myth and the social novel gave us shared reality, and we are losing it
points: The great works are about the world with the author absent; they build a common imagination a society can argue within.
A culture of 'lived experience' as the only authority ends in relativism — no overall story, only competing testimonies.
Confessional culture feeds and is fed by social media's incentives; literature should resist them, not ratify them.
objections: Epics are full of selves — Odysseus lies about himself for a living; the Iliad is one man's rage.
The 'shared' story was shared by those allowed to tell it; nostalgia for it is nostalgia for a narrower canon.
Nobody chose this fashion in a vacuum: readers want it, and wanting the personal is itself a shared pattern worth reading.

speakers.name: Rebecca Goldstein
speakers.stance: Philosopher and novelist (Plato at the Googleplex; Betraying Spinoza) who writes about 'mattering' — the need to matter beyond oneself. Likely to argue that the self only makes sense inside larger stories, without dismissing the personal.

speakers.name: Patricia Lockwood
speakers.stance: Author of the memoir Priestdaddy and the internet novel No One Is Talking About This; writes from the self and the feed with formal daring. Expect a defence of the personal as a way into the universal, delivered with jokes.

speakers.name: Emily Wilson
speakers.stance: Translator of the Odyssey and Iliad; has written on how epics are communal, performed and full of individual voices. Likely to argue the ego/epic opposition is a false one and that Homer already contains both.

speakers.name: Shahidha Bari
speakers.stance: Hosts. Academic, critic and broadcaster (Front Row; Dressed).

questions: What is the last novel with no author-figure in it that changed how you see the world?
If the epic gave a society its shared story, what is our shared story now — and who is telling it?
Is the difference between memoir and autofiction one of truth, or just of the contract with the reader?

reading.title: The Odyssey
reading.note: The translation that made the epic feel spoken — read Book 9, where Odysseus tells his own story.

reading.title: No One Is Talking About This
reading.note: The self, the feed, and then grief — the case for the personal in one book.

reading.title: The Mind–Body Problem
reading.note: Her first novel: philosophy carried by a very particular self.

terms.def: Fiction that uses the author's own life and name as material while claiming the freedoms of the novel.
Long narrative poetry of a culture's foundational stories — Gilgamesh, Homer, Virgil — usually performed, communal, and impersonal in voice.
First-person testimony as a source of knowledge and authority — celebrated as inclusion, criticised as unarguable.

30.question: Are the educated no longer winning — and if degrees have stopped paying, is the fault with education or with our idea of it?
30.why: Graduate premiums are shrinking, student debt is at record levels and AI is aimed squarely at the cognitive skills universities sell. Whether the answer is more trades, less school, or a different kind of education decides what a generation is told to do at eighteen.

sides.label: The future belongs to the skilled and self-taught; mass higher education was a bubble
points: For many degrees the lifetime earnings bounce is now smaller than the debt; electricians and plumbers out-earn graduates in their twenties.
Knowledge is free and instant; three years memorising it is a signalling ritual, not learning.
Illich's charge stands: compulsory schooling teaches conformity and the habit of being taught, not judgement.
objections: Averages hide the point: the premium collapsed for some subjects and institutions, not for education as such.
AI automates the routine skills first — trades are not immune, and the judgement that survives is exactly what good education builds.
The self-taught who succeed are the survivors we hear about; most people learn better with structure and teachers.

sides.label: Education isn't failing; a factual, credential-driven version of it is. Rebuild it around judgement
points: Wisdom to choose between facts is more valuable when facts are free, not less; that was always the point of a liberal education.
The debt crisis is a financing model, not an argument against learning.
Societies that abandoned broad education for narrow skills paid later in adaptability.
objections: 'Judgement' is what every curriculum reform has promised since Dewey; the results are hard to measure and easy to fake.
Rebuilding around judgement may just mean the elite keeps the good education while everyone else is steered into 'skills'.
Knowledge-rich schooling produced the very graduates now said to be losing; the diagnosis contradicts the evidence.

speakers.name: Daniel Susskind
speakers.stance: Oxford economist (A World Without Work; Growth: A Reckoning) who has argued that AI will hollow out cognitive work and that education must be rethought rather than expanded on autopilot.

speakers.name: Thangam Debbonaire
speakers.stance: Labour peer, former MP and professional musician. Likely to defend access to education and lifelong learning while conceding that the funding model is broken.

speakers.name: Michael Gove
speakers.stance: As Education Secretary he championed a knowledge-rich curriculum in the E. D. Hirsch tradition and academic rigour. Expect a defence of knowledge against 'skills-only' thinking and a critique of what universities did with their autonomy.

speakers.name: Philip Collins
speakers.stance: Hosts. Columnist and former chief speechwriter to Tony Blair.

questions: If a degree is a signal, what would you replace it with that employers would trust?
Which is more likely to survive AI: a plumber's apprenticeship or a philosophy degree — and why?
Should the state stop subsidising degrees that don't pay, or is that a market test that education was never meant to pass?

reading.title: Deschooling Society
reading.note: The argument, cited in the billing, that schooling manufactures conformity.

reading.title: A World Without Work
reading.note: His case on automation and what humans are left to do.

reading.title: The Case Against Education
reading.note: The strongest economic version of 'it's mostly signalling'.

terms.def: The extra lifetime earnings from a degree over the alternative — now negative for some courses once debt is counted.
The theory that credentials mainly certify pre-existing ability and conscientiousness rather than adding skills.
Schooling built on a defined body of facts and cultural literacy, as opposed to generic skills.

33.question: Should we deliberately engineer the planet's climate — or is 'dominion over nature' the delusion that caused the crisis?
33.why: Solar geoengineering is now funded by billionaires and debated in Nature; carbon removal is written into net-zero plans. As warming outruns emissions cuts, the question moves from whether to research it to who decides, on what evidence, and what happens if it stops.

sides.label: We are already engineering the planet — badly. Doing it on purpose may be the only responsible option
points: Emissions are not falling fast enough; reflecting a fraction of sunlight is the one lever that works on the timescale of the damage.
Refusing to research it doesn't stop it; it guarantees that when a desperate government tries it, no one will know what they're doing.
Humans have taken planetary responsibility for good and ill since agriculture; the honest position is to manage it consciously.
objections: Solar geoengineering doesn't remove carbon: it masks warming while oceans acidify, and stopping it abruptly is catastrophic ('termination shock').
Regional effects — monsoons, droughts — fall on people who had no vote; there is no governance for a global thermostat.
Moral hazard: a cheap-looking fix weakens the will to cut emissions.

sides.label: Geoengineering is the Enlightenment delusion at planetary scale; the answer is transformation, not control
points: The crisis came from treating nature as a machine to be optimised; the same mindset cannot be the cure.
The risks are unbounded and irreversible, the benefits accrue to those who caused the problem, and the technology entrenches their power.
Cutting emissions, restoring ecosystems and changing economies are proven; stratospheric aerosols are a bet.
objections: 'Transformation' has been the plan for thirty years while emissions rose; refusing a tool on philosophical grounds has costs measured in lives.
Rejecting all intervention is itself a decision to accept whatever warming arrives.
Nature restoration and carbon removal are also engineering; the line between wise and hubristic is being drawn by preference.

speakers.name: Adrienne Buller
speakers.stance: Author of The Value of a Whale, a critique of green capitalism and market fixes. Expect scepticism of techno-solutions that leave the economic system intact.

speakers.name: Janos Pasztor
speakers.stance: Former UN assistant secretary-general and head of the Carnegie Climate Governance Initiative, which pushed for rules on geoengineering research without advocating deployment. Expect 'we must govern it before someone does it' rather than either camp.

speakers.name: Adam Frank
speakers.stance: Astrophysicist (Light of the Stars) who frames humanity as a planetary force that must learn to steer its 'technosphere'. Likely to argue that conscious management of the planet is now unavoidable.

speakers.name: Laurie Laybourn
speakers.stance: Researcher on climate 'derailment risk' and co-author of Planet on Fire, arguing for systemic economic change. Likely to warn that geoengineering distracts from and entrenches the causes.

speakers.name: Isabel Hilton
speakers.stance: Hosts. Journalist and founder of China Dialogue.

questions: Who should be able to veto a solar geoengineering programme — and who would actually be able to?
If research is fine but deployment isn't, what stops research from becoming deployment?
Is planting a forest engineering the planet? Where exactly does dominion begin?

reading.title: Under a White Sky
reading.note: The best reported tour of deliberate planetary intervention and its ironies.

reading.title: The Value of a Whale
reading.note: Her critique of market and technological climate fixes.

reading.title: Light of the Stars
reading.note: His argument that civilisations and planets co-evolve — the frame he'll bring.

terms.def: Reflecting sunlight, typically with stratospheric aerosols, to cool the planet without removing carbon.
Rapid warming if a solar geoengineering programme were stopped while greenhouse gases remain high.
A safety net that encourages riskier behaviour — here, a fix that weakens emissions cuts.

41.question: Is the universe a law-governed mechanism, or an evolving, self-creating process whose 'laws' are themselves history?
41.why: Cosmology's puzzles — why these laws, why these constants, why a universe hospitable to life — have led serious physicists to propose that laws evolve, are selected, or were not fixed at the start. It is a fight over what a fundamental explanation even looks like.

sides.label: The laws are timeless and universal; finding them is what physics is
points: Relativity and quantum mechanics predict to a dozen decimal places; no evolutionary story has produced a single number.
'Evolving laws' either obey a deeper fixed rule (so the laws aren't really evolving) or nothing (so there is no explanation at all).
Selection needs variation and inheritance across many universes we cannot observe; that is metaphysics with equations.
objections: Fixed laws cannot explain themselves: why these laws, these constants, this initial state?
The 'unreasonable effectiveness' of mathematics may be a selection effect of what physicists choose to study.
Physics already accepts that effective laws change with energy and epoch; 'timeless' is an assumption, not a finding.

sides.label: The cosmos evolves: laws, constants and even time emerged, and selection is the deepest explanation we have
points: Hawking's final theory with Hertog: the laws we see crystallised in the early universe from a broader range, the way biology's rules emerged.
Smolin's cosmological natural selection makes a testable claim — that universes are tuned to make black holes.
Evolution explains complexity without a designer or a lawgiver; that is exactly the explanatory gap cosmology has.
objections: Darwinian selection needs competing populations; one universe, or unobservable others, is not a population.
'Explains without predicting' is what the billing itself concedes; physics has always demanded more.
Evolving laws may just push the question back: what governs the evolution?

speakers.name: Thomas Hertog
speakers.stance: Stephen Hawking's collaborator and author of On the Origin of Time, which argues the laws of physics evolved in the early universe and should be read 'top-down' from our position. Expect the strongest case that laws have a history.

speakers.name: Daniel Whiteson
speakers.stance: CERN experimental particle physicist and co-author of We Have No Idea. Likely to defend the empirical, law-seeking method while cheerfully admitting how much remains unknown.

speakers.name: Ivette Fuentes
speakers.stance: Experimental quantum physicist working on quantum sensors and relativistic quantum information. Likely to ask what any 'evolving laws' picture would let us measure.

speakers.name: Philip Ball
speakers.stance: Hosts. Science writer and former Nature editor.

questions: What observation would show that a law of physics has changed — and has anyone made one?
If laws evolved, was there ever a moment with no laws? What did that look like?
Is 'the universe is an organism' a theory, an analogy, or a mood?

reading.title: On the Origin of Time
reading.note: Hawking's final cosmology as Hertog tells it — the position he brings.

reading.title: The Singular Universe and the Reality of Time
reading.note: The philosophical case that laws evolve and time is real.

reading.title: We Have No Idea
reading.note: Whiteson's guide to the unknowns — and his temperament.

terms.def: Smolin's proposal that universes reproduce through black holes, so physics is tuned to make many of them.
Hawking and Hertog's idea that our observations select which histories of the universe are relevant, rather than one history running forward from the start.
The observation that small changes to physical constants would make life impossible — the puzzle both sides claim to solve.

42.question: Have nation states already surrendered sovereignty to Big Tech — and can they take it back?
42.why: Governments run on Amazon and Microsoft clouds, elections play out on Meta and Alphabet's feeds, and one company's satellites decide battlefield communications. The debate is whether regulation is still possible or whether states are now junior partners.

sides.label: The state has already lost: infrastructure, discourse and even war run through a few firms nobody elected
points: 60% of government cloud data sits on two American companies; that is not a supplier relationship but a dependency.
Platforms shape what three billion people see, with no oversight comparable to broadcasting law.
Firms now make sovereign decisions — restricting Starlink in wartime, refusing military uses — and states accept it because they must.
objections: States retain the monopoly on law and force; a company can be broken up, taxed, or banned the moment a government is willing to bear the cost.
Dependency runs both ways: the same firms depend on states for spectrum, courts, contracts and protection.
The story confuses American corporate power with the end of the nation state; Europe and China are already writing different rules.

sides.label: Sovereignty is intact if states use it: regulate, diversify, and stop outsourcing judgement
points: The EU's Digital Services and Markets Acts, China's platform crackdown and Australia's news bargaining code show states can bite.
Procurement is policy: governments chose the cheapest cloud; they can choose sovereign or federated ones.
Bans are blunt but real — India banned TikTok overnight, Brazil suspended X.
objections: Regulation is slow, captured and always a generation behind the product.
Bans and 'sovereign' infrastructure impose real costs on citizens and often protect state surveillance more than liberty.
Fines in the billions are a rounding error for firms worth trillions; the rules are priced in.

speakers.name: Silkie Carlo
speakers.stance: Director of Big Brother Watch; campaigns against surveillance by states and corporations alike. Expect resistance to both Big Tech power and to 'sovereignty' that means state control over speech — the civil-liberties position between the two.

speakers.name: Leo Varadkar
speakers.stance: Former Taoiseach of Ireland, the European home of most US tech firms. Likely to argue that states can regulate through the EU while acknowledging the economic dependence of small countries.

speakers.name: Sebastian Mallaby
speakers.stance: Author of The Power Law on venture capital and a biography of Demis Hassabis. Likely to argue that tech power is real but that markets and states remain the more durable forces.

speakers.name: Michael Gove
speakers.stance: Former Cabinet minister and Spectator editor; a nation-state sovereigntist who supported the Online Safety Act. Expect the case that states must and can reassert control over platforms.

speakers.name: Roger Hearing
speakers.stance: Hosts. Journalist and broadcaster, formerly of the BBC World Service.

questions: Which government has actually taken power back from a platform, and what did it cost its citizens?
If Anthropic can veto a military use of its software, is that corporate overreach or exactly the check we'd want?
Would you rather your government's data sat with Microsoft or with your own government? Why?

reading.title: The Age of Surveillance Capitalism
reading.note: The influential case that platforms have accumulated a new kind of power.

reading.title: The Power Law
reading.note: How venture capital built the firms in question — Mallaby's ground.

reading.title: Digital Empires
reading.note: The American, Chinese and European models of governing tech, compared.

terms.def: A state's control over the data, infrastructure and platforms its citizens depend on.
The EU's Digital Services Act (content and platform duties) and Digital Markets Act (curbs on gatekeeper firms).
Weber's definition of the state: the sole legitimate user of force in a territory.

48.question: Is boredom the route to a self and an inner life — or a luxury nostalgia for a world where entertainment was rationed?
48.why: Attention is the most contested resource of the decade. Neuroscience of the default mode network gives the 'rest builds the self' intuition a mechanism, while the digital-detox industry turns it into a product. The question is whether constant stimulation costs us something real.

sides.label: Constant stimulation hollows the self; boredom is where identity and thought are made
points: The default mode network, active in wakeful rest, is where autobiographical memory and self-reflection happen; feeds suppress it.
Creativity research consistently finds insight follows unstructured time; a life without gaps is a life without ideas.
The economics are revealing: the wealthy buy silence, retreats and phone-free schools while selling stimulation to everyone else.
objections: The neuroscience is suggestive, not causal — nobody has shown scrolling erases the self.
Boredom in history meant drudgery and isolation, not creative reverie; its romance is a class privilege.
People have always feared new media would corrode the mind; the novel was once the infinite scroll.

sides.label: Entertainment on demand is a triumph — the problem is exploitation of attention, not stimulation as such
points: Access to music, film, argument and community that once belonged to the rich is now universal; that is not a loss.
The self is made in engagement with others and the world, not in an empty room.
Blame the business model that farms attention, not the human appetite for stories.
objections: Designed compulsion is not the same as chosen pleasure; 'we love it' is what the metrics were built to produce.
The universal abundance is thin: a hundred tabs is not a rich inner life.
Even if the appetite is ancient, the dose is new — and the harm data on sleep, attention and adolescence keeps accumulating.

speakers.name: Patricia Lockwood
speakers.stance: Novelist of the feed (No One Is Talking About This); lives in the internet and is ambivalent about it. Expect neither detox sermon nor techno-cheer, but a precise account of what the scroll does to a mind.

speakers.name: Jordan Stephens
speakers.stance: Musician (Rizzle Kicks), author of the memoir Avoidance, Drugs, Heartbreak and Dogs, and mental-health advocate. Likely to speak for rest, boredom and stepping away, from experience.

speakers.name: Tony D. Sampson
speakers.stance: Digital-culture theorist (Virality; A Sleepwalker's Guide to Social Media) who argues platforms work through affect and contagion below conscious attention. Expect a critique of Big Tech's grip on experience.

speakers.name: Jay Shapiro
speakers.stance: Hosts. Philosopher and podcaster (Dilemma).

questions: When did you last do nothing for an hour — and did anything happen?
Is 'protect your attention' advice for individuals, or a way of letting the platforms off?
If boredom is a luxury good, who is being asked to give up the entertainment they only just got?

reading.title: Stolen Focus
reading.note: The popular case that attention is being taken from us, with the research and its critics.

reading.title: A Philosophy of Boredom
reading.note: Boredom as a modern condition — the longer view.

reading.title: A Sleepwalker's Guide to Social Media
reading.note: Sampson's account of how platforms work on us below awareness.

terms.def: Brain regions most active during rest and mind-wandering, linked to self-reflection and memory.
Business built on capturing and reselling attention, so engagement is engineered.
Deliberate time away from screens — now a multi-billion industry, which is part of the argument.

50.question: Is ageing a disease we can defeat — and if we could postpone death indefinitely, should we want to?
50.why: Senolytics, rapamycin trials and one man's public $2m-a-year protocol have moved life extension from Gilgamesh to clinical research. The argument is scientific (does the biology allow it?) and philosophical (what would a life without an end be for?).

sides.label: Ageing is damage, damage can be repaired, and death from old age is an engineering problem
points: Mice live 40% longer with senescent cells cleared; every ageing pathway identified so far is a target, not a mystery.
We already treat the diseases of ageing one at a time; treating the process is the same project done honestly.
'Death gives life meaning' was invented to console people who had no choice; nobody argues the same about cancer.
objections: Mouse results have a poor record of translating; the human data for life extension is, so far, nil.
Even perfect repair leaves accident, violence and the second law; 'indefinite' postponement is marketing.
A therapy available first to the very rich would create a biological class divide unlike any before.

sides.label: The immortality quest is an ancient fantasy in a lab coat — impossible, and not even desirable
points: Gilgamesh, the alchemists, the Immortalisation Commission of 1920s Russia: the dream recurs because it is a refusal of the human condition, not a research programme.
Swift's Struldbruggs are the answer: endless life without endless youth is a curse, and endless youth is a self that never changes.
Meaning depends on finitude — commitment, courage, generations — and a society of the undying would be a society of the entrenched.
objections: Every extension of life expectancy so far was called unnatural and then welcomed; 80 is not the sacred number.
Nobody proposes forcing longevity on anyone; the argument against research is an argument to deny others a choice.
'Meaning needs death' is asserted by people who plan to live to 90; ask them at 60.

speakers.name: Aubrey de Grey
speakers.stance: Biogerontologist behind the SENS damage-repair approach and the idea of 'longevity escape velocity'. Expect the full engineering case that ageing is curable and that the first person to live to 1,000 may be alive.

speakers.name: Bryan Johnson
speakers.stance: Tech founder behind 'Blueprint' and the Don't Die movement, publicly measuring every biomarker. Joins from California; expect data, protocols and a moral case for treating death as the enemy.

speakers.name: John Gray
speakers.stance: Philosopher whose The Immortalization Commission traced how science took over religion's promise to abolish death. Expect the argument that the quest is a secular religion and a flight from the human.

speakers.name: Sarah Wilson
speakers.stance: Author (First, We Make the Beast Beautiful; This One Wild and Precious Life), critical of wellness and techno-optimism. Likely to argue for accepting mortality and for meaning over metrics.

speakers.name: Güneş Taylor
speakers.stance: Hosts. Geneticist and science communicator.

questions: What is the strongest human evidence — not mouse evidence — that ageing can be slowed?
If the treatment existed, who gets it first, and what happens to a democracy of people who never leave?
What would you do with year 300 that you couldn't do with year 80?

reading.title: The Immortalization Commission
reading.note: His history of science's attempts to cheat death — the frame he'll use.

reading.title: Ending Aging
reading.by: Aubrey de Grey and Michael Rae (2007)
reading.note: The SENS programme laid out.

reading.title: Gulliver's Travels, Part III (the Struldbruggs)
reading.note: The short, devastating case that living forever is not the same as staying young.

terms.def: Aged cells that stop dividing but linger, secreting inflammatory signals; clearing them ('senolytics') extends mouse lifespans.
The point at which each year of research adds more than a year of life expectancy.
The more modest goal: shortening the years of ill health before death rather than adding years.

51.question: Do superpowers still run the world — or is 'great powers dividing the globe' a fairytale in an age of many hands on the wheel?
51.why: Iran and Ukraine have humbled bigger powers; Taiwan's fabs and Egypt's canal hold leverage no navy can seize; half of trade runs outside the blocs. Whether fragmentation means danger or opportunity decides how middle powers should play the next decade.

sides.label: Power has fragmented for good: many centres, more leverage for the rest, a shared future if we manage it
points: Chips, chokepoints, demographics and commodities give small and middle powers vetoes the Cold War never allowed.
The Global South's refusal to pick sides over Ukraine shows the blocs no longer command loyalty.
Multipolarity has kept the peace in Southeast Asia for decades; it can be organised, not just feared.
objections: Fragmentation without rules is the 1930s: every previous multipolar system ended in general war.
Leverage is not power — Taiwan's chips make it a target as much as a player.
The 'rest' are hedging because they are weak, not because they are winning.

sides.label: The great powers still decide; the rest adapt. Pretending otherwise is dangerous
points: Only the US and China can project force globally, print reserve currency, or set technology standards.
Europe learned in 2022 what dependence on someone else's security guarantee costs.
Middle-power 'autonomy' is real only until a great power decides it isn't.
objections: The US could not bend Iran, Afghanistan or the Houthis; Russia could not take Kyiv. 'Deciding' has a poor recent record.
China's demographic decline and America's political volatility make both an uncertain anchor.
Great-power framing is self-serving: it is how the great powers describe a world that is slipping from them.

speakers.name: Kishore Mahbubani
speakers.stance: Former Singaporean ambassador and UN Security Council president; author of Has China Won? and The Asian 21st Century. Expect the argument that the West must adjust to an Asian-led, multipolar world, made with a diplomat's polish.

speakers.name: Kwasi Kwarteng
speakers.stance: Former Chancellor and historian of empire (Ghosts of Empire; War and Gold). Likely to argue that power remains concentrated and that Britain and the West should be realistic about their weight.

speakers.name: Leo Varadkar
speakers.stance: Former Taoiseach; the small-state, EU-embedded perspective. Likely to argue that pooled sovereignty is how small nations survive a multipolar world.

speakers.name: Mary Ann Sieghart
speakers.stance: Hosts. Journalist and author of The Authority Gap.

questions: Name a decision in the last five years that a great power wanted and a smaller one blocked. What does it prove?
If multipolarity is dangerous, is the alternative Chinese or American hegemony — and which would you choose?
What should a country of five million actually do differently in a fragmented world?

reading.title: Has China Won?
reading.note: His case that America is losing a contest it barely admits it's in.

reading.title: The Tragedy of Great Power Politics
reading.note: The realist theory that great powers cannot help competing.

reading.title: Ghosts of Empire
reading.note: Kwarteng's history of how imperial power actually worked — and unravelled.

terms.def: Several centres of power rather than one (unipolar) or two (bipolar).
A state too small to dominate but large enough to shape outcomes — Australia, Türkiye, Indonesia, Brazil.
A physical or technological bottleneck (Suez, Taiwanese fabs, Dutch lithography) that confers leverage out of proportion to size.

58.question: Are grand philosophical systems coming back — and can we even avoid having one, whether or not we admit it?
58.why: Analytic piecemeal work, Wittgenstein's silence and postmodern suspicion all declared the total account of the world dead. Yet every science, ideology and 'anti-metaphysics' relies on a framework it rarely states. The debate is whether to build one deliberately or refuse on principle.

sides.label: We can't escape metaphysics, so we should do it well: the overall account returns
points: Every claim presupposes a picture of what claims are, what the world is, and how the two meet; refusing to state it just leaves it unexamined.
Postmodernism itself was a system — a theory of language, power and meaning — that pretended not to be one.
The sciences are fragmenting; only a philosophical account can say how physics, biology and mind fit together.
objections: Systems from Hegel to Marx ended in totalising politics; the suspicion of grand accounts was earned.
A framework is not a system: we can hold background assumptions provisionally without a cathedral.
Every system so far has been refuted; 'this time we'll get it right' is what every system said.

sides.label: The complete account is hubris; philosophy's job is to clear confusions and stay piecemeal
points: Wittgenstein's point stands: the demand for a view of the whole is a picture holding us captive, not a task.
Local, revisable, problem-by-problem progress is how every successful inquiry works.
Claims to an overall account have always turned out to be one tradition's assumptions dressed as everyone's.
objections: 'Stay piecemeal' is itself an overall stance about what philosophy is and can do.
Refusing a framework doesn't remove one; it hands the job to physics or the market by default.
The confusion-clearing project has run for a century without agreement on what was cleared.

speakers.name: Hilary Lawson
speakers.stance: Author of Closure: A Story of Everything — an explicit overall account in which language 'closes' an open world. Expect the case that the systematic ambition is unavoidable and that his own theory shows it can be done without dogma.

speakers.name: Divya Dwivedi
speakers.stance: Indian philosopher (with Shaj Mohan, Gandhi and Philosophy; Indian Philosophy, Indian Revolution) working in the deconstructive tradition and against caste. Likely to be suspicious of systems as vehicles of power, while insisting philosophy must 'begin again'.

speakers.name: Sebastian Rödl
speakers.stance: Idealist philosopher (Self-Consciousness and Objectivity) who defends an absolute idealism in the Hegelian line. Expect the strongest case that a systematic account of thought and world is not just possible but required.

speakers.name: Danielle Sands
speakers.stance: Hosts. Philosopher working in continental philosophy and literature.

questions: State, in one sentence, the framework you're relying on tonight. If you can't, is that modesty or evasion?
What went wrong with Hegel and Marx — the systems, or what people did with them?
Is a scientist who says 'only physics is real' doing metaphysics? Badly?

reading.title: Closure: A Story of Everything
reading.note: The system on the table.

reading.title: Philosophical Investigations
reading.note: The case against the demand for a view of the whole — sections 89–133 especially.

reading.title: Self-Consciousness and Objectivity
reading.note: Rödl's short, dense argument for absolute idealism.

terms.def: The account of what fundamentally exists and how it hangs together — declared dead by positivists and postmodernists, and now contested.
The tradition from Russell and Moore onwards favouring logical analysis and piecemeal problems over systems.
Lawson's term for the way language and thought make a definite world out of an 'open' one.

59.question: Has 'mental health' become an industry that medicalises ordinary distress — or is this the first era with real treatment for real suffering?
59.why: Antidepressant prescribing and therapy spending keep rising while measured rates of depression and anxiety don't fall — the 'treatment-prevalence paradox'. Whether that means the treatments don't work, the wrong people get them, or distress is being manufactured decides how billions are spent.

sides.label: We have medicalised life: distress is a response to circumstances, not a disease, and the industry profits from calling it one
points: The serotonin story behind antidepressants has collapsed (the 2022 umbrella review); the drugs' effects are small and hard to separate from placebo and withdrawal.
Diagnoses have expanded to cover grief, shyness and adolescence; one in three women prescribed antidepressants is a cultural fact, not an epidemic of brain disease.
Treatment has risen for decades without prevalence falling — the paradox the billing cites — which is what you'd expect if the model is wrong.
objections: The paradox has other explanations: more people recognising distress, treatment reaching the wrong people, or social conditions worsening faster than treatment helps.
'Natural response to life' is cold comfort to someone who cannot get out of bed; critics rarely say what they'd offer instead.
Disputing the serotonin story does not show the drugs don't work; the trials show modest benefit, and modest benefit across millions is large.

sides.label: Mental illness is real, treatable, and under-treated; scepticism costs lives
points: Depression has biology — inflammation, sleep, genetics — and biological treatments help, as do therapies with strong evidence bases.
The alternative to treatment historically was not resilience but silence, shame and suicide.
Rising diagnosis reflects falling stigma; that people seek help is a success, not a scandal.
objections: If treatment works and reaches more people every year, why does the population not get better?
A vocabulary in which every difficulty is a 'condition' can teach helplessness — the argument that awareness campaigns raise reported symptoms.
Biology of distress is not the same as disease: stress also inflames; grief also changes the brain.

speakers.name: Joanna Moncrieff
speakers.stance: Psychiatrist and critic of the biomedical model (The Myth of the Chemical Cure), lead author of the 2022 review finding no consistent link between serotonin and depression. Expect the strongest case that antidepressants are over-sold and distress is not a brain disease.

speakers.name: Edward Bullmore
speakers.stance: Cambridge neuropsychiatrist and author of The Inflamed Mind, linking depression to inflammation. Likely to defend biological psychiatry while agreeing the old chemical-imbalance story was too simple.

speakers.name: Mark Solms
speakers.stance: Neuroscientist and psychoanalyst (The Hidden Spring) who argues feelings are the foundation of consciousness. Expect a middle path: distress has biology, but it is meaningful and about something.

speakers.name: Sarah Wilson
speakers.stance: Author of the anxiety memoir First, We Make the Beast Beautiful, sceptical of the wellness industry while speaking from experience. Likely to challenge both the treatment machine and easy dismissals of suffering.

speakers.name: Jonny Thomson
speakers.stance: Hosts. Philosophy writer (Mini Philosophy).

questions: If antidepressant effects are small and hard to separate from placebo, why do so many patients report they helped?
What is the line between distress that should be treated and distress that should be lived through — and who draws it?
If treatment rates doubled again, what would you predict happens to prevalence?

reading.title: 'The serotonin theory of depression: a systematic umbrella review'
reading.note: The paper that reset the argument; read the responses too.

reading.title: The Inflamed Mind
reading.note: The biological case, newer than serotonin.

reading.title: The Hidden Spring
reading.note: Solms's theory of feeling and consciousness.

terms.def: The observation that rising treatment rates have not reduced the population prevalence of depression and anxiety.
Redefining ordinary experiences as medical conditions requiring treatment.
The claim that depression is caused by low serotonin — widely publicised, now widely disowned.

67.question: Does desire need prohibition — and did sexual liberation, by removing the limits, remove the thrill?
67.why: Openness has never been greater and sex has never been rarer: a third fewer adults having weekly sex than in 1990, a quarter of young adults having none. Bataille and Lacan predicted this. The question is whether limits are the engine of desire or a romance of repression.

sides.label: Prohibition is the engine: eroticism needs transgression, desire needs lack, and total permission is deflating
points: Bataille: the erotic is the violation of a taboo; remove the taboo and you remove the charge.
Lacan: desire is structured by what is missing; abundance and instant availability starve it.
The data fit: the most liberated generation is the least sexually active, and pornographic abundance coincides with reported anhedonia.
objections: Correlation with phones, precarity, later partnering and loneliness explains the decline without invoking metaphysics of taboo.
'Reinstate limits' has no mechanism that isn't coercive; you cannot legislate mystery.
Repression's golden age had plenty of sex — and rape, shame and unwanted pregnancy. The nostalgia is selective.

sides.label: Liberation was right; what's missing is intimacy, time and conditions, not taboo
points: Liberation freed women, gay people and the unmarried from real harm; that gain is not up for renegotiation.
Desire flourishes with safety, consent and communication; the recent decline tracks economic and social stress, not permissiveness.
Mystery and limits can be chosen inside freedom — boundaries between two people, not imposed on a society.
objections: 'Chosen limits' concedes the point: desire needs limits; the argument is only about who sets them.
Consent culture, however necessary, can turn seduction into a negotiation — a change in kind, not just in safety.
If liberation worked, the numbers should be rising, not falling.

speakers.name: Dasha Nekrasova
speakers.stance: Actor (Succession) and co-host of the Red Scare podcast, known for contrarian, post-liberal takes on sex and culture. Likely to argue that liberation flattened desire and that limits and mystery matter.

speakers.name: Farha Khalidi
speakers.stance: Feminist commentator with a large TikTok following. Likely to defend liberation, consent and openness and to resist any return to prohibition.

speakers.name: Agnieszka Piotrowska
speakers.stance: Filmmaker and psychoanalytic theorist (director of Married to the Eiffel Tower; author on psychoanalysis and the ethics of encounter). Expect the Lacanian account of desire and lack, argued from film and clinical theory.

speakers.name: Güneş Taylor
speakers.stance: Hosts. Geneticist and science communicator.

questions: What is a limit on desire that isn't a limit on someone's freedom?
If liberation is to blame, why is the decline sharpest among people who grew up after it was complete?
Is porn abundance a prohibition problem or a supply problem?

reading.title: 'Why Are Young People Having So Little Sex?'
reading.note: The reported piece behind the 'sex recession' numbers.

reading.title: Sexual Revolution
reading.note: A feminist defence of liberation — Penny speaks in Sunday's Grown Up debate.
